q: What is the primary operational advantage of an MLV core vaccine over a killed vaccine in a congregate shelter?
o: MLV is stable at room temperature for months
MLV gives a faster onset of protective immunity (hours to days), whereas killed needs a booster 2 to 4 weeks later to protect
MLV can be mixed in one syringe with antibiotics
MLV faces no maternal antibody interference
e: MLV replicates in the host for rapid immunity; killed vaccines need a primary plus booster to protect, which is too slow for shelter disease control.

q: A shelter core combination product should contain:
o: Only MLV core components
Core plus Leptospira and Bordetella for broad cover
Whatever the manufacturer will combine on request
Rabies mixed with the core MLV
e: Shelter core combos should be MLV core only; rabies is monovalent killed and not mixed, and non-core agents are not routinely included.

q: Roughly what proportion of dogs are unprotected against CPV-2, CDV or both on shelter intake?
o: About 10%
About 30%
About 64.5%
Over 95%
e: About 64.5% of dogs are unprotected against CPV-2, CDV or both on intake, which is why vaccinating at entry matters.

q: Mucosal (intranasal or oral) vaccines are recommended for respiratory pathogens because they:
o: Produce systemic IgG only, lasting years
Develop local URT humoral and cellular immunity within 3 to 7 days
Cannot be given to naive animals
Are always killed products
e: Mucosal products generate rapid local respiratory-tract immunity (3 to 7 days), useful against respiratory pathogens, especially in naive animals.

q: A distinct advantage of recombinant (vectored) vaccines is that they:
o: Replicate fully in the host like MLV
Express the target antigen without replicating the pathogen, may work better through MDA, and (being non-adjuvanted) carry reduced injection-site sarcoma risk
Require no cold chain
Provide lifelong immunity after one dose for all diseases
e: Recombinant vaccines present antigen without pathogen replication, can perform better against MDA, and avoid adjuvant-related sarcoma risk in cats.

q: Which is a recognized cause of vaccine failure?
o: Administering MLV core on intake
Maternal antibody interference, improper storage or handling, exposure before full immunization, or waning immunity
Using the labeled volume
Vaccinating a healthy adult
e: Failure stems from host non-response, pre-immunization exposure, MDA, cold-chain or handling errors, waning immunity, and manufacturing faults.

q: A 5-week-old stray puppy enters during a parvovirus outbreak. The correct core schedule while in the shelter is:
o: A single MLV dose at intake, then boosters every 6 months
An MLV core vaccine at intake, repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks of age
Wait until 12 weeks so maternal antibody clears, then vaccinate once
Two killed doses 14 days apart, then stop
e: Serial MLV boosting every 3 to 4 weeks to 16 to 20 weeks closes the window of vulnerability as maternal antibody wanes.

q: Why are juveniles revaccinated at short intervals until 16 to 20 weeks?
o: To exhaust the bone marrow of inflammatory cells
So that as soon as maternal antibody falls below the blocking threshold in an individual, the next dose can immunize
Because juveniles clear vaccine antigen within 48 hours
To prevent lifelong environmental allergies
e: Maternal antibody declines at individual rates; frequent dosing ensures a dose lands once the animal becomes immunizable.

q: The window of vulnerability is best defined as the period when maternal antibody is:
o: High enough to protect and to allow immunization
Too low to protect against virulent virus but still high enough to block vaccine immunization
Absent, so the animal is fully protected
Only relevant to killed vaccines
e: A virulent virus overcomes maternal antibody more readily than vaccine virus, creating a gap where the animal is susceptible yet not immunizable.

q: Regarding vaccination of very young neonates:
o: MLV should be given on day 1 of life
Neither MLV nor killed vaccine should be given in the first 2 weeks of life
Killed vaccine is safe from birth
Colostrum has no effect on early vaccine response
e: Before 2 weeks the immune system cannot respond well and vaccine virus can cause disease; colostral IgG also blocks active immunity in the first days.

q: To conserve maternal antibody, a shelter considers delaying puppy vaccination. The correct guidance is:
o: Delay until 16 weeks to preserve passive immunity
Do not delay vaccination to conserve maternal antibody; vaccinating while it is present does not speed its decline
Vaccinate the nursing dam instead to protect the litter
Give a single dose and skip boosters
e: Vaccination should not be delayed to spare maternal antibody, and vaccinating the dam does not protect nursing juveniles.

q: The canine core vaccines for a shelter are:
o: Leptospira, Borrelia and rattlesnake toxoid
Canine parvovirus, distemper, adenovirus-2 and rabies
Microsporum canis, Giardia and Malassezia
Tetanus toxoid, Streptococcus equi and CIV
e: Core protects against the severe, contagious pathogens (CPV, CDV, CAV-2 and rabies); the others are non-core or not vaccine targets.

q: The shelter MLV DA2PP schedule for pups is:
o: A single dose at 12 weeks only
At or before entry from 4 weeks, with boosters every 2 to 3 weeks until 18 to 20 weeks
One dose at intake and one at 1 year
Killed product every 6 weeks
e: MLV DA2PP starts at 4 weeks at intake and boosts every 2 to 3 weeks to 18 to 20 weeks; adults get an intake dose plus a 2 to 3 week booster.

q: Rabies vaccination of shelter dogs should be given:
o: To every dog on intake regardless of age
As a single parenteral dose to all dogs over 12 weeks before release (on entry only if a long stay is anticipated)
Only if the dog shows respiratory signs
Mixed into the DA2PP syringe
e: In-shelter rabies exposure is low, so it is timed to release for public health, given to dogs over 12 weeks, and not combined with core MLV.

q: Why is an intranasal Bordetella-only product discouraged in favor of a two-way intranasal Bordetella and CPIV vaccine?
o: Bordetella-only products are not refrigerated
A dog at risk for Bordetella is also at risk for CPIV, so both should be covered
Intranasal routes are blocked by maternal antibody
CPIV is not a shelter concern
e: Risk overlaps, and intranasal products avoid maternal antibody interference while giving rapid local immunity, so the two-way product is preferred.

q: Regarding parvovirus susceptibility in puppies, which statement is correct?
o: All pups are protected once they receive any single dose
Maternal antibody can persist 13 to 15 weeks, so all pups under 18 to 20 weeks should be considered susceptible regardless of vaccines received
Parvovirus immunity is always partial like distemper
Pups over 8 weeks need no further doses
e: Maternal antibody can block vaccine for 13 to 15 weeks; parvovirus immunity is all-or-none, so young pups remain potentially susceptible until 18 to 20 weeks.

q: Which vaccine group is considered non-core and low priority for routine shelter use?
o: MLV DA2PP and rabies
Leptospira, canine influenza and Lyme
Intranasal Bordetella and CPIV
Parenteral rabies
e: Leptospirosis, canine influenza and Lyme pose minimal in-shelter risk and are not part of the routine shelter program.

q: Why is a standard MLV FPV vaccine contraindicated in a pregnant queen?
o: It causes anaphylaxis in most pregnant cats
The live virus can cross the placenta and damage the fetal cerebellum, causing cerebellar hypoplasia
It permanently stops colostrum production
It turns the coat white
e: MLV panleukopenia virus targets rapidly dividing fetal cerebellar cells; in an outbreak the maternal and litter risk may still outweigh this, but a killed product is safer in pregnancy.

q: To mitigate injection-site sarcoma consequences, feline vaccines should be given:
o: Into the interscapular scruff for comfort
Into the flank midway between ribs and hip
As distally on a limb as possible, or in the tail, to allow complete surgical margins if a sarcoma develops
Into the jugular furrow
e: Distal-limb or tail placement permits curative amputation with clean margins; scruff and flank are no longer recommended.

q: A 2.5 cm firm nodule is found at a rabies vaccine site 6 weeks after injection. By the 1-2-3 rule the next step is:
o: Re-check in 6 months with warm compresses
Biopsy or aspirate now, because the mass is 2 cm or larger
Massage with isopropyl alcohol
Start oral corticosteroids and assume it is benign
e: The 1-2-3 rule triggers biopsy if a post-vaccinal mass is 2 cm or larger, persists 3 months, or is still growing at 1 month; 2.5 cm meets the size criterion.

q: The shelter FVRCP schedule for kittens is:
o: A single dose at 8 weeks only
A dose at intake as early as 4 weeks, then boosters every 2 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks
Killed FVRCP every 6 months
Intranasal FPV preferred over parenteral
e: Kittens get FVRCP from 4 weeks at intake with boosters every 2 weeks to 16 to 20 weeks; intranasal FPV is not preferred for panleukopenia protection.

q: Which statement about FCV and FHV-1 vaccination is correct?
o: It prevents infection completely
Immunity develops in about 7 days, but vaccination does not prevent infection and instead reduces disease severity
It eliminates latent FHV-1 infection
It is a core vaccine only for cats over 5 years
e: Respiratory core immunity is partial: it lessens severity but does not prevent infection, and FHV-1 latency persists.

q: Correct use of the feline FeLV vaccine includes:
o: A single dose gives full protection
Testing FeLV status first and giving 2 doses 3 to 4 weeks apart, since a single dose provides no protection
Giving it only to FeLV-positive cats
Mixing it with FVRCP in one syringe
e: FeLV status is checked first; two doses 3 to 4 weeks apart are required because a single dose does not protect (it is core for cats under 1 year).

q: After rabies vaccination, protective immunity is induced and lasts:
o: Within hours, lasting 6 months
As early as 2 to 3 weeks, with a minimum DOI of 3 years for most products
Only after three doses, lasting 1 year
Immediately, lasting 10 years
e: Killed adjuvanted rabies vaccine induces immunity in 2 to 3 weeks with a minimum 3-year DOI (up to 4 years for one feline product).

q: Comparing 1-year and 3-year rabies products in shelters:
o: The 1-year product is always safer
The 3-year product is as safe or safer and is recommended, especially in shelters
Only the 1-year product is legal
They cannot be used in cats
e: The 3-year product is as safe or safer and is preferred; it is acceptable for cats, as is the non-adjuvanted 1-year recombinant feline vaccine.

q: For shelter dogs, rabies vaccine should be administered:
o: To all dogs on intake regardless of age
As a single parenteral dose to all dogs over 12 weeks before release
Only to dogs staying under 48 hours
By any volunteer
e: Because in-shelter exposure is limited, rabies is timed to release for dogs over 12 weeks, with on-entry use only for long stays.

q: An adult dog with no prior rabies history receives its first rabies dose at the shelter. Legally it must be:
o: Never revaccinated if a 3-year product was used
Revaccinated within the year in most communities, regardless of whether a 1-year or 3-year product was used
Titer-tested instead of revaccinated
Revaccinated only if it bites someone
e: Animals without prior rabies vaccination must be revaccinated within a year in most jurisdictions; staff should communicate this to adopters.

q: Rabies is an exception to which general core-vaccine rule?
o: It must be MLV
Although killed, it protects after a single dose and may be given at an interval under 2 weeks from other cores
It must be given on intake
It cannot be given to cats
e: Rabies breaks the killed 2-dose-within-6-weeks rule and the 2-week minimum spacing, protecting most animals over 3 months after one dose.

q: A box of MLV FVRCP was left on a counter at room temperature for about 36 hours. The correct action is:
o: Refrigerate and use as normal
Discard it, because live attenuated virus degrades out of the cold chain and the vaccine is now ineffective
Combine two doses per syringe to compensate
Autoclave and use as a killed product in pregnancy
e: MLV is heat-sensitive; reconstituted or warmed product out of the cold chain (over an hour at room temperature) must be discarded.

q: A healthy dog with no clinical signs has a negative CDV and CPV titer during an outbreak. It should be classified and managed as:
o: Low risk, kept in the general population
High risk, removed from the general population immediately
Indeterminate, no action needed
Immune, adopted at once
e: A negative titer with no signs means likely susceptibility, so the animal is high risk and is separated from the population.

q: For risk assessment in puppies and kittens, the better testing approach is:
o: A qualitative in-house kit, because the cut-off is set for juveniles
Quantitative (lab) titer testing, because it can distinguish active immunity from passive maternal antibody
No testing, since juveniles are always low risk
Antigen testing rather than antibody testing
e: Qualitative kits cannot separate active from passive immunity in juveniles, so quantitative titers are the gold standard, and passive low-risk status can change as maternal antibody wanes.

q: How does recent vaccination affect FeLV versus FIV point-of-care testing?
o: Both become unreliable for 2 weeks
FeLV antigen testing is unaffected, but FIV antibody testing cannot reliably distinguish vaccine from infection
FIV testing is unaffected, but FeLV becomes falsely positive
Neither test is ever affected by vaccination
e: FeLV tests detect antigen and are unaffected, while FIV tests detect antibody that vaccination also produces, so vaccinated and infected cats are hard to distinguish (PCR may help).

q: A mild to moderately ill but stable dog needs core vaccination on intake. The guidance is:
o: Never vaccinate any ill animal
Vaccinate now, since vaccines are unlikely to harm while virulent exposure is the greater danger, and repeat no less than 2 weeks after recovery
Wait 8 weeks regardless of recovery
Vaccinate only after a full chemistry panel
e: For mild to moderate illness, vaccinate on intake (virulent exposure is the bigger risk) and repeat at least 2 weeks after recovery; only animals too ill to vaccinate safely are handled separately in isolation.

q: During a canine parvovirus outbreak, which statement about vaccinating already-exposed dogs is correct?
o: Vaccinating infected dogs worsens disease severity
Vaccinating does not worsen disease; all dogs should receive MLV DA2PP immediately regardless of exposure status
Exposed dogs should be quarantined for 14 days before vaccinating
Vaccination during an outbreak is contraindicated until the outbreak resolves
e: Vaccinating an already-infected animal does NOT worsen disease. All animals should be vaccinated at entry during a CPV outbreak regardless of exposure history.

q: During a CPV outbreak, a healthy 12-week-old pup received two DA2PP doses (at 6 and 9 weeks). How should this pup be managed?
o: It is fully protected — keep in the general population
It should be treated as potentially susceptible; maternal antibody can persist to 13–15 weeks and may have blocked both prior doses
Place in isolation as it is definitely infected
Vaccinate once more then consider immune
e: All pups under 18–20 weeks must be treated as potentially susceptible regardless of vaccination history, because MDA can persist to 13–15 weeks and block vaccine response.

q: Which CDV outbreak characteristic makes early vaccination uniquely valuable compared to CPV or FPV?
o: CDV vaccines take 6 weeks to produce any immunity
Partial CDV immunity can develop within days of a single MLV dose, unlike CPV/FPV where immunity is all-or-none and takes longer
CDV is only spread by contact so vaccination is not urgent
CDV vaccines must be killed products to avoid outbreak interference
e: CDV is unique in providing early partial immunity within days of a single MLV dose. CPV and FPV immunity is all-or-none and takes longer to develop. This makes fast CDV vaccination especially impactful.

q: During a feline panleukopenia outbreak, which vaccine product is preferred for all cats ≥4 weeks?
o: Killed (inactivated) FVRCP, because it is safest for all cats including pregnant queens
Intranasal MLV FVRCP, because mucosal immunity develops within 24 hours
Parenteral MLV FVRCP, because it provides the best protection against FPV in an outbreak
Any available FPV product — efficacy is equivalent across all formulations
e: Parenteral MLV FVRCP is the preferred product in an FPV outbreak. Intranasal MLV and killed FVRCP provide less reliable panleukopenia protection. Killed products are safer in pregnancy but used only if parenteral MLV is unavailable.

q: Which disinfectant FAILS against both CPV and FPV outbreaks?
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (AHP) 1:32
Potassium peroxymonosulfate (Virkon) 1%
Quaternary ammonium compounds (quats)
Sodium hypochlorite 1:32
e: Quaternary ammonium compounds fail against both CPV and FPV (non-enveloped viruses). AHP, potassium peroxymonosulfate, and bleach (1:32) are effective with adequate contact time.

q: What is the primary advantage of the recombinant canarypox-vectored CDV vaccine (rCDV) over MLV CDV in an outbreak setting?
o: It requires no refrigeration
It does not contain live CDV so it does not interfere with PCR diagnostics, and it may perform better through maternal antibody
It provides lifetime immunity after a single dose
It can be mixed with MLV DA2PP in the same syringe for efficiency
e: rCDV does not contain replicating CDV, so PCR tests remain interpretable for outbreak diagnosis. It may also perform better through maternal antibody, making it useful for young pups in outbreak settings.

q: The minimum temperature monitoring equipment required in a vaccine storage refrigerator is:
o: A standard dial thermometer mounted on the fridge door
A min/max thermometer placed in the center of the fridge
A digital display built into the fridge itself
Daily staff visual inspection of the fridge without a dedicated thermometer
e: A min/max thermometer (not a dial gauge or built-in display) is the minimum standard — it records the highest and lowest temperature since last reset, capturing excursions that a point-in-time reading would miss.

q: A shelter discovers on Monday morning that the vaccine fridge alarm shows a high-temperature excursion over the weekend. The correct immediate action is:
o: Discard all vaccines immediately to prevent liability
Quarantine the affected stock with a 'Do Not Use' label and contact the vaccine manufacturer for lot-specific guidance before discarding or using
Vaccinate all animals in the queue immediately before the vaccines degrade further
Move vaccines to the freezer to preserve them
e: Contact the manufacturer — do not discard immediately. Manufacturers have stability data for specific time-temperature combinations; the vaccines may still be viable depending on duration and temperature reached. Moving vaccines to a freezer can damage killed-product adjuvants and MLV components.

q: What is the correct use-time limit for a reconstituted MLV vaccine at room temperature?
o: 4 hours, same as killed vaccines
24 hours if kept covered and away from light
30–60 minutes; discard any unused portion after this time
The entire working day if kept capped and refrigerated after use
e: Reconstituted MLV vaccine must be used within 30–60 minutes and discarded. Killed vaccines are more thermostable (use within 4 hours out of the fridge), but reconstituted MLV cannot be returned to the refrigerator for later use.

q: During a power failure, vaccines should be immediately transferred to:
o: A regular household freezer to slow vaccine degradation
An insulated cooler with ice packs (not loose ice), targeting 2–8°C (36–46°F)
A warm environment so vaccines are ready for immediate use
A second fridge in a different building with the same temperature setting
e: Ice packs (not direct loose ice) in an insulated cooler maintain 2–8°C (36–46°F). Loose ice can freeze and damage vaccines. Freezing kills adjuvants in killed products and damages MLV components.
